result.markdown: # Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions {#i-ep02 .unnumbered} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 2, you can - fit and interpret a multiple regression with dummies, interactions, and curves - compare nested models and test groups of terms with a partial F-test - read a regression table from a research paper and state its limits ::: Tutorials are exam preparation sessions. The tasks below are exam-style questions. You first try each task in pairs. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. Then the class discusses the solution together. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 4 and 5. Lecture 6 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Use the complete [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) while working. If needed, review [Mathematics Refresher: indicators and reference categories](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#indicators-and-reference-categories), [products, interactions, and combined effects](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#products-interactions-and-combined-effects), and [polynomial terms](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#polynomial-terms). Complete from memory: 1. You interpret a multiple-regression slope while ... 2. A dummy coefficient compares ... 3. An interaction coefficient is a difference in ... 4. A partial F-test compares ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. Holding the other included predictors fixed. 2. A category with the named reference category. 3. Slopes. 4. A reduced nested model with a complete model on the same observations. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial Try each task in R before you open the answer. Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). First build the data for the analysis. The code is the same as in Lectures 4--6. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group), ref = "all_men") known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) ``` ::: ### Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With all 1,441 pitches (`sharks`), fit a regression of the equity offered, in percent (`equity_offered_pct`), on the season (`season`), the requested amount in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`), and the number of words in the description (`description_words`). Then answer these questions. 1. Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are held fixed. 2. Find out which 95% confidence interval of a coefficient includes zero. 3. Interpret adjusted $R^2$ and the overall F-test. 4. Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks ) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.295 -4.776 -1.283 3.288 82.106 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 22.0249310 0.8878522 24.807 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8361515 0.0509825 -16.401 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028975 0.0005771 -5.021 5.79e-07 *** description_words -0.1283379 0.1137527 -1.128 0.259 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.619 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1876, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 110.6 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. Among the 1,441 recorded pitches, at fixed values of the other included predictors: - one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less equity offered, on average - an extra \$1,000 requested is associated with about 0.0029 percentage points less (about 0.29 points per \$100,000), on average - one additional description word is associated with about 0.128 percentage points less, on average. 2. `confint(m1)` shows that the interval for the description words, about $(-0.351, 0.095)$, includes zero. 3. $R^2\approx0.188$: the model explains about 19% of the variation in the equity offered. Adjusted $R^2\approx0.186$ is almost the same, so the fit does not come from extra predictors that only fit chance variation. The overall F-test ($F\approx110.6$ on 3 and 1437 df) rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero. 4. Any two of these: only selected pitches reach the show, the quality of the venture is not measured, the equity offered may influence the amount requested, and the variables may be measured with error. ::: ### Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5) Use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`). Fit a reduced model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`). Fit a complete model that adds the team category `gender` (all-men, all-women, or mixed). Compare the two models with `anova()`. 1. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Name the reference category. 2. Interpret both dummy coefficients. 3. State the hypotheses of the partial F-test and decide. 4. Explain why the partial F-test and the individual t-tests answer different questions. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) summary(complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.118 -4.778 -1.100 3.220 82.590 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 20.8388333 0.5064929 41.143 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8238940 0.0477959 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0026613 0.0005822 -4.571 5.28e-06 *** genderall_women 1.2835231 0.4810241 2.668 0.00771 ** gendermixed 0.1209343 0.5411539 0.223 0.82320 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.612 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1913, Adjusted R-squared: 0.189 F-statistic: 84.49 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(reduced, complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1431 83228 2 1429 82792 2 436.25 3.7649 0.0234 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. The reference category is all-men. 2. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men teams, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more. The unit is percentage points, not percent. The categories are broad and the data do not come from an experiment, so the result does not show a causal effect of gender. 3. $H_0$: both dummy coefficients are zero. $H_1$: at least one of them is not zero. $F\approx3.76$ and p $\approx$ 0.023, so reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The two terms are jointly significant. 4. The t-test of the mixed dummy alone (p $\approx$ 0.82) is far from significant, but the F-test rejects. The F-test asks whether the two terms together improve the model. Each t-test asks about one comparison with the reference category. ::: ### Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6) With the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`), fit a regression of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the centred season `season_c`, the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed teams), their interaction, and the requested amount (`ask_1k`). 1. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and for `women = 1` at the average requested amount. 2. Calculate both season slopes. 3. Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value without claiming too much in either direction. 4. Explain what centring does. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_interaction <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(m_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.871 -4.742 -1.290 3.412 82.689 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 13.6247907 0.3354522 40.616 < 2e-16 *** season_c -0.7993817 0.0663226 -12.053 < 2e-16 *** women 0.8069665 0.4117061 1.960 0.0502 . ask_1k -0.0026776 0.0005834 -4.590 4.83e-06 *** season_c:women -0.0614594 0.0955667 -0.643 0.5203 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1894, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1871 F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. At the average requested amount, the fitted line for all-men teams is $12.866-0.799\,\text{season\_c}$, and for teams with women it is $13.673-0.861\,\text{season\_c}$, as in Lecture 6. The intercept 12.866 is the intercept 13.625 plus the `ask_1k` coefficient times the average requested amount, `mean(known_gender$ask_1k)`. For teams with women the intercept is $12.866+0.807=13.673$. 2. The season slope is about $-0.799$ percentage points per season for all-men teams. For teams with women it is $-0.7994-0.0615\approx-0.861$. 3. The estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per season, with p $\approx$ 0.520. The model gives no evidence that the season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. 4. Centring makes the `women` coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate. ::: ### Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6) With all 1,441 pitches (`sharks`), fit a linear model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`), and a quadratic model that adds the square of `season`, written `I(season^2)`. Compare the two models with `anova()`. 1. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Why must you write `I(season^2)` in the R formula? 2. Decide with the partial F-test whether the quadratic term improves the model. 3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11. 4. State why you should not extrapolate the curve beyond Season 16. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks) m_quadratic <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks ) summary(m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.154 -4.549 -1.011 3.390 82.000 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.171681 0.820566 29.457 < 2e-16 *** season -1.713233 0.205669 -8.330 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.051034 0.011369 4.489 7.74e-06 *** ask_1k -0.002711 0.000574 -4.723 2.56e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.57 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1981, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1965 F-statistic: 118.3 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_linear, m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1438 83493 2 1437 82338 1 1154.5 20.149 7.737e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. `I()` tells R to calculate the square. Without `I()`, R would read `^` as part of the formula syntax and not as a square. 2. $H_0$: the coefficient of the quadratic term is zero. The partial F-test gives $F\approx20.1$ with p $<$ 0.001, so reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The quadratic term improves the model. 3. With $\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713$ and $\hat\beta_2\approx0.051$, the change from Season 10 to 11 is $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times10+1)=\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2\approx-0.64$ percentage points. Never read $\hat\beta_1$ alone while the quadratic term is in the model. 4. Beyond Season 16 the fitted curve turns upward, and no data support that turn. A quadratic curve can change direction sharply outside the observed range. ::: ### The models of Tasks 2 to 4 in one table {#iep02-spec-table} [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 4 showed how research papers put several models side by side in one regression table. The table below does this for the models of Tasks 2 to 4. All columns of such a table must use the same observations. Tasks 2 and 3 use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`). Task 4 uses all 1,441 pitches. So first fit the quadratic model again on the 1,434 pitches. The code then prints the two model outputs that the answers above do not show. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_quadratic_known <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(reduced) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.169 -4.814 -1.136 3.277 82.219 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 21.1849717 0.4838230 43.787 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8152726 0.0472948 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028517 0.0005776 -4.937 8.87e-07 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.626 on 1431 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.187, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 164.6 on 2 and 1431 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(m_quadratic_known) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.160 -4.540 -1.010 3.401 82.003 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.1677366 0.8217246 29.411 < 2e-16 *** season -1.7128060 0.2059832 -8.315 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.0509421 0.0113830 4.475 8.24e-06 *** ask_1k -0.0026921 0.0005749 -4.682 3.10e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.576 on 1430 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1982, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1966 F-statistic: 117.9 on 3 and 1430 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Column (1) is the reduced model of Task 2 (`reduced`), column (2) the complete model of Task 2 (`complete`), column (3) the interaction model of Task 3 (`m_interaction`), and column (4) the quadratic model (`m_quadratic_known`). ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) | |:---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Season | −0.815\*\*\* | −0.824\*\*\* | −0.799\*\*\* | −1.713\*\*\* | | | (0.047) | (0.048) | (0.066) | (0.206) | | Season squared | | | | 0.051\*\*\* | | | | | | (0.011) | | Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.0029\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | | | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | | All-women team | | 1.284\*\* | | | | | | (0.481) | | | | Mixed team | | 0.121 | | | | | | (0.541) | | | | Team with women (all-women or mixed) | | | 0.807 | | | | | | (0.412) | | | Season × team with women | | | −0.061 | | | | | | (0.096) | | | Intercept | 21.185\*\*\* | 20.839\*\*\* | 13.625\*\*\* | 24.168\*\*\* | | | (0.484) | (0.506) | (0.335) | (0.822) | | Observations | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | | $R^2$ | 0.187 | 0.191 | 0.189 | 0.198 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.186 | 0.189 | 0.187 | 0.197 | ::: Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. All four columns use the same 1,434 pitches with a known team classification. The reference category is all-men teams. In column (3) season is centred at its mean (about 8.8), so the intercept and the coefficient of "Team with women" refer to the average season. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. Read along the Season row. The coefficient is close to $-0.8$ in columns (1) to (3). In column (4) it is $-1.713$, because with the quadratic term in the model the season coefficient alone is not the trend. Read down a column to see one model. Columns (2), (3), and (4) each add terms to column (1), so a partial F-test can compare each of them with column (1). The bottom rows show that the four models fit almost equally well: adjusted $R^2$ lies between 0.186 and 0.197, a difference of about one percentage point of the variation in the equity offered. Use this layout for regression results in your thesis. ### Task 5: Read a regression table from a paper The table below is invented. It has the layout of a table in a research paper, the same layout as the table above. The outcome is entrepreneurial intention on a scale from 1 to 7, measured in a survey of 265 students. Self-efficacy is a score from 1 to 7 for how confident a student is that he or she can start a business. The table does not show the intercept. Some journals do this. ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | |:---|---:|---:| | Age (years) | 0.02 | 0.01 | | | (0.02) | (0.02) | | Female (1 = yes) | −0.21\* | −0.15 | | | (0.10) | (0.10) | | Prior entrepreneurial experience (1 = yes) | | 0.42\*\* | | | | (0.13) | | Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1--7) | | 0.38\*\*\* | | | | (0.07) | | Observations | 265 | 265 | | $R^2$ | 0.03 | 0.19 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.02 | 0.18 | ::: Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. 1. What do the numbers in parentheses and the stars mean? Check the stars of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t statistic. The critical value is $t_{0.975,\,260}$ = `qt(0.975, 260)` = 1.969. 2. Interpret the self-efficacy coefficient in column (2) in one complete sentence. 3. The coefficient of Female changes from $-0.21$ with a star in column (1) to $-0.15$ without a star in column (2). Explain what happened with the ideas of Lecture 4, and say what the missing star does and does not mean. 4. $R^2$ rises from 0.03 to 0.19. What does that say, and which test would show whether the two added predictors are jointly significant? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. The numbers in parentheses are standard errors. The stars show the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero. For self-efficacy, $t_{obs}=0.38/0.07\approx5.4$. This is far beyond the critical value $t_{0.975,\,260}$ = `qt(0.975, 260)` = 1.969, and p is below 0.001, so three stars are correct. 2. Among the 265 surveyed students, a self-efficacy score that is one point higher is associated with an entrepreneurial intention that is 0.38 points higher, holding age, gender, and prior experience fixed. 3. Model (2) holds two more variables fixed than model (1). The Female coefficient now compares women and men with the same experience and self-efficacy. In column (1), at the same age, the difference between women and men was 0.21 points. Part of this difference went together with differences in experience and self-efficacy. The missing star says that the confidence interval around $-0.15$ includes zero. It does not show that the difference is zero. 4. The two added predictors explain a further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this sample. A partial F-test of the two nested models would show whether the two added predictors are jointly significant. It compares model (1) with model (2) on the same 265 students. If you have the data, `anova()` of the two fitted models gives this test. ::: ### Task 6: A/B test, one-way ANOVA, moderator and mediator (Lectures 5 and 6) (a) An invented A/B test. An online shop for refurbished phones shows 120 new visitors either its current product page (`new_page = 0`) or a new page with customer videos (`new_page = 1`). Chance decides which page each visitor sees, 60 visitors per page. The outcome is the value of the first order in euros. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(21) # random assignment: 60 zeros (old page) and 60 ones (new page) new_page <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = 60)) # invented order values in euros, with a true effect of 3 euros order_value <- round(40 + 3 * new_page + rnorm(120, mean = 0, sd = 8), 2) ab_shop <- data.frame(new_page, order_value) ``` ::: Regress `order_value` on the treatment dummy `new_page`. Test in five steps whether the new page changes the mean order value. The critical value is $t_{0.975,\,118}$ = `qt(0.975, 118)` = 1.980. Explain why $\hat\beta_1$ estimates the average treatment effect of the new page, and judge its size. (b) An invented one-way ANOVA. The same shop records the delivery time in hours of 20 orders for each of three couriers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(7) courier <- factor(rep(c("cycle", "post", "van"), each = 20)) delivery_hours <- round(c(rnorm(20, 20, 6), rnorm(20, 26, 6), rnorm(20, 22, 6)), 1) deliveries <- data.frame(courier, delivery_hours) ``` ::: Fit the regression of `delivery_hours` on `courier` and make its ANOVA table with `anova()`. Which dummies does this regression use? What do its two dummy coefficients say? Test at 5% whether the mean delivery time is the same for the three couriers. Give $H_0$, $F$, both degrees of freedom, and the conclusion. The critical value is `qf(0.95, 2, 57)` = 3.16. (c) A meal-kit start-up gives a discount coupon at random to half of its customers. Customers with the coupon order more meal kits. The coupon raises orders more for students than for other customers. The coupon also brings customers to the website more often, and more visits go with more orders. Which variable is a moderator, and which is a mediator? How does each one appear in a regression of orders on the coupon dummy? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer (a) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ab_fit <- lm(order_value ~ new_page, data = ab_shop) summary(ab_fit)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 39.086333 0.9480553 41.22790 6.427869e-72 new_page 3.409333 1.3407527 2.54285 1.228932e-02 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} qt(0.975, df = 118) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.980272 ``` ::: ::: The mean order value is 39.09 euros with the old page (the intercept) and $39.09+3.41=42.50$ euros with the new page. 1. **Hypotheses.** $H_0:\beta_1=0$, the new page has no effect on the mean order value. $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%. 2. **Test statistic.** $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with $df=n-k-1=118$. 3. **Critical value and rejection region.** $t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$, from `qt(0.975, df = 118)`. Reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.980$. 4. **Observed value.** $t_{obs}=3.409/1.341\approx2.54$. 5. **Conclusion.** $2.54\ge1.980$, so reject $H_0$ (p $\approx$ 0.012). At the 5% level, the new page raises the mean order value. Chance decided who saw the new page. So the two groups are alike on average in everything else, measured or not, and the only systematic difference is the page. That is why $\hat\beta_1\approx3.41$ euros estimates the average treatment effect of the new page. It is about 8.7% of the mean order value with the old page. (b) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} courier_fit <- lm(delivery_hours ~ courier, data = deliveries) coef(courier_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) courierpost couriervan 22.650 3.935 -0.015 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(courier_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: delivery_hours Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) courier 2 207.25 103.623 2.9512 0.06031 . Residuals 57 2001.40 35.112 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(deliveries$delivery_hours) # overall mean ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 23.95667 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} qf(0.95, 2, 57) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.158843 ``` ::: ::: The ANOVA table comes from the regression of `delivery_hours` on two dummies, `post` and `van`, with `cycle` as the reference category. The intercept 22.65 hours is the mean of the cycle courier. The post courier takes on average 3.94 hours longer, and the van courier 0.02 hours less. 1. **Hypotheses.** $H_0:\mu_{\text{cycle}}=\mu_{\text{post}}=\mu_{\text{van}}$. $H_1$: at least one mean differs. The significance level is 5%. 2. **Test statistic.** $F$ = mean square of `courier` divided by the mean square of the residuals, with $G-1=2$ and $n-G=57$ degrees of freedom. 3. **Critical value and rejection region.** The critical value is 3.16, from `qf(0.95, 2, 57)`. Reject $H_0$ if $F_{obs}\ge3.16$. 4. **Observed value.** $F_{obs}=103.62/35.11\approx2.95$. 5. **Conclusion.** $2.95<3.16$ (p $\approx$ 0.060), so do not reject $H_0$. At the 5% level, the data do not show that the mean delivery time differs between the couriers. This does not prove that the means are equal. The largest difference, 3.95 hours between the post and the van courier, is about 16% of the overall mean of 23.96 hours. (c) - Student status is the moderator: it changes the slope of the coupon. It enters as an interaction, `lm(orders ~ coupon * student)`, and the coefficient of `coupon:student` is the difference in the coupon effect between students and other customers. - Website visits are the mediator: they lie on the path from the coupon to orders. Adding visits, `lm(orders ~ coupon + visits)`, shrinks the coupon coefficient to the direct part. For the total effect of the coupon, leave visits out of the model. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Individual practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Build one model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) in the Shark Tank file.
